questions.prompt: Match each indicator to its colour in a BASE.
questions.explain: Every indicator has its own colour code.

questions.prompt: What colour does china rose indicator turn in an ACID?
questions.explain: China rose: dark pink in acids, green in bases.

questions.prompt: Why can't turmeric be used to identify an acid?
options: Turmeric stays yellow in both acids and neutral solutions

feedback.2: Turmeric turns red in BASES, not acids.

questions.explain: Turmeric only changes in bases, so it can't tell acids from neutral substances.

questions.prompt: Sort the indicators: natural or synthetic (made in a lab)?
questions.explain: Natural indicators come from plants or lichens; synthetic ones are made in labs.

questions.prompt: A solution turns phenolphthalein pink. What can you conclude?
options: It could be acidic or neutral
questions.explain: Phenolphthalein turns pink only in bases.

questions.prompt: A solution leaves phenolphthalein colourless. Which conclusion is BEST?
options: It is acidic or neutral, so another test is needed
questions.explain: Phenolphthalein is colourless in both acids and neutral solutions. Use another indicator (e.g. blue litmus) to decide.

questions.text: Indicators that change smell instead of colour, such as onion and vanilla, are called ___ indicators.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order to make a china rose indicator.
steps: Collect a few china rose petals
Wait until the water becomes coloured
Test the coloured liquid with an acid and a base

questions.prompt: A yellow haldi stain on a shirt turns red when washed with soap. Why?
options: Soap is a base and turmeric is an indicator
questions.explain: Soap is basic; turmeric turns red-brown in bases.

questions.prompt: You have three colourless liquids: an acid, a base and water. You only have red litmus. How can you identify all three?
questions.modelAnswer: Dip red litmus in each. The one that turns it blue is the base. Then add a drop of that base to the other two. Or: use the now-blue litmus paper from the base: dip it in the remaining two; the one that turns it red again is the acid and the one with no change is water.
rubric: Red litmus turning blue identifies the base
I found a clever way to tell the acid from water (e.g. reuse the blue litmus)
questions.explain: Thinking creatively about limited tools is a key science skill.
